masthead_title: The AI selloff gave stocks their worst week since June, and oil closed back above $100.
regime_line: Stocks had their worst week since June (S&P 500 −1.95%, Nasdaq Composite −4.48%) as AI stocks kept falling and oil closed back above $100, while the 10-year Treasury yield fell 15bp on the week to 5.09% (tightening).
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one expired, three open, two new

Every open conditional claim (§4B — a specific, falsifiable test this system logs before the outcome is known, then grades against the data) is checked against the latest closes and prints before any new narrative is written. Closes and credit prints are recorded in data/raw/claims_check_2026-10-19.json.

story_html:
The press called last week an AI-debt scare plus an oil shock. The Associated Press reported that the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both had their worst week since June, and that chip companies “pulled back some more as worries deepened about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last.” Reuters’ closing headline read “Wall Street ends down sharply; worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh.” Reuters tied the AI selloff to concerns that “debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.” CNBC’s close: “Nasdaq slides 2% Friday to post worst week since June, pressured by AI sell-off and oil prices.” The Wall Street Journal’s and Financial Times’ own pages couldn’t be reached from this system’s search, so their framing isn’t reported.

What the data confirms, and what it complicates. The size checks out. The S&P 500 fell 1.09% Friday and 1.95% for the week; the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.15% and 4.48%. In this system’s own closes, both are the worst weeks since the one that ended June 26. The chip fund SMH fell 3.41% Friday and 10.53% for the week. But the “borrowing costs” part needs care. Treasury yields fell: the 2-year 3bp Friday, the 10-year 15bp for the week. And the broad junk-bond spread (dated Thursday) slipped 2bp to 3.23%. So the higher borrowing costs in the press accounts show up in specific AI builders’ debt (Tier 3), not in Treasuries or the broad junk index, at least through Thursday’s print. Friday’s credit print, due tonight, tests whether that changed (CL-0048).

The average stock did better than the index again. On Friday the equal-weight RSP fell 0.42% against 1.11% for the cap-weighted SPY. For the week, RSP rose 0.49% while SPY fell 1.97%. The Russell 2000 of smaller companies fell 1.66% to its lowest close since April 16, now 11.31% below its Aug 14 high. Even the 10-year’s drop leaves it high: it has been at or above 5.09% since Sep 23. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007 (Today in history, below).

Oil and the weekend: supply mechanics only. WTI rose 3.51% Friday to $101.41, up 10.41% for the week. That is its first close above $100 since Sept 18 and its highest since Sept 17 (this system’s closes). CNBC led with “Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries.” Reuters, citing the shipping-data firm Kpler, reported that the seven-day average of Gulf crude flows fell to about 8.5 million barrels a day last week, from more than 20 million the week before. Over the weekend, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two laden tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, and Iranian media reported another on Sunday, per Reuters. None of the incidents has been independently confirmed. Reuters also reported that Iran’s foreign minister said Tehran’s offer to reopen the strait within six days still stands, on conditions that include lifting the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. AFP and CNBC reported that a Ukrainian drone attack set fires at oil facilities in St. Petersburg, according to the city’s governor. And CNBC and CBS reported that an executive order signed late Friday waived the Graham Act’s new Russia sanctions and tariffs just before they took effect, including tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian crude and gas. As mechanics, that removes a threatened penalty on buyers of Russian oil. Reuters’ Monday oil headline: “Oil slips from 5-month high as Trump’s Russia sanctions waiver may bring more supplies.” This brief takes no side on any of these policies; it tracks what they do to supply and prices.

This morning. CNBC’s Sunday-evening blog led with “Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade.” Reuters reported Monday that stock futures were climbing as AI stocks rebounded, with oil and Treasury yields lower, and that Intel rose about 4% before the open after JPMorgan upgraded it to neutral from underweight. Futures move all morning, so no level is quoted here. Why this matters: last week hit the most popular, most borrowed corner of the market hardest, while bonds rallied and the average stock held up. That is a concentrated selloff, not a broad one, so far.
dashboard_interp_html:
Rates eased again on Friday and fell for the week. The 10-year slipped 1bp to 5.09% (z +1.54), the 2-year 3bp to 4.74% (z +1.62) and the 3-month bill 2bp to 4.26% (z +2.11). The 30-year held at 5.43% (z +1.29). For the week, the 10-year fell 15bp, the 30-year 17bp and the 2-year 6bp, so long-term yields fell most. Falling yields with long-term rates leading is a bull flattener (Unit 1). The 2s10s spread (the 10-year minus the 2-year) is 35bp, 12bp narrower over five sessions.

High against the last 30 years, average against the full record. The 3-month bill sits at the 52nd percentile since 1981 and the 71st over the last 30 years. The 2-year sits at the 52nd percentile since 1976 and the 82nd over 30 years. The 10-year sits at the 47th percentile since 1962 and the 84th over 30 years. The 30-year sits at the 47th percentile since 1977 and the 83rd over 30 years.

Thursday’s real-yield split is in, and it cuts against the oil story. On Thursday the 10-year fell 9bp. The 10-year real yield (what a Treasury pays after inflation, dated 10-15) fell 6bp to 2.78%, and the 10-year breakeven (the bond market’s inflation forecast) fell 3bp to 2.32%. So on a day of hot producer prices and a 3% oil gain, the bond market’s inflation forecast went down, not up (Unit 2). CL-0047 tests whether oil above $100 changes that this week.

Credit held near Wednesday’s level. HY OAS (dated 10-15, Thursday’s rally day) eased 2bp to 3.23% (z +3.36, still the day’s largest flag). Only two readings in the past six months were wider: Wednesday’s 3.25% and Oct 1’s 3.24%. It sits at the 75th percentile of its own ~3-year record here: unusual lately, upper-middle on its short full record. IG OAS (the investment-grade version, dated 10-15) held at 0.84% (z +1.88). Friday’s selloff-day print arrives tonight (CL-0048).

The dollar (DXY) eased 0.16% to 101.84 (z +1.49, just below the flag line): the 71st percentile since 1971 and the 80th over 30 years. SOFR (the overnight bank funding rate, dated 10-15) was 3.89% (z +2.28), still in the 3.85%–3.90% range it has held since the Fed’s September hike. ON RRP (money funds’ overnight parking spot at the Fed) fell to $0.10 billion. The Fed balance sheet and TGA are unchanged until Thursday’s report.

Why this matters: bonds did their job last week. The 10-year fell 15bp while the Nasdaq fell 4.48%, so a balanced portfolio’s bond side cushioned the stock side. Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year, so borrowers got a little relief. The credit piece is the one to watch: if the junk-spread print dated 10-16, due tonight, shows widening, that would suggest the AI-debt worry is spreading beyond a few borrowers (CL-0048).
history_html:
The level, and the run. The 10-year fell to 5.09%, below this run’s 5.31% peak of Oct 5, but it has been at or above 5.09% since Sep 23. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007. Against the last 30 years that’s high (84th percentile); since 1962 it’s average (47th).

July 2007, then vs. now. Long-term rates match: 5.11% then, 5.09% now. Short-term rates don’t. The Fed’s rate was 5.25% then; SOFR is 3.89% now, so the 3-month-to-10-year spread is +83bp against +14bp then. The S&P 500 was at a record that day; today it’s 2.04% below one.

Oil’s year, in context. WTI is up 76.6% this year, the largest gain through this date in the 26 years of futures data here. It is still 30.2% below its 2008 record close. So this is an unusually fast year for oil, not an unusually high price.

The speed is in two-year yields. The 2-year is up 127bp this year, the 9th-largest rise through this date in 50 years. A 12-month rise this big (1.33 points) has started 8 times since 1977. From each start, stocks were lower a year later in 3 of 8, against 24.4% for any 12-month stretch. A recession began within two years in 2 of 8, against 27.4% normally. Eight is a small sample.

Why this matters (client-ready): “Long-term rates are back at mid-2007 levels, and oil has had its fastest year in our data, but corporate borrowing spreads are still tight on the longest record we have. When two-year rates rose this fast before, stocks were lower a year later in 3 of 8 cases, versus about one in four normally: a small sample, not a forecast.”
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically (503 of 503 covered, plus all 50 megacaps); a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest), never by seeming interesting. 51 name candidates and 7 sector divergences qualified; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note. No company-specific Friday catalyst (earnings, guidance or a downgrade) surfaced for any big decliner, so the outlets’ group-level framing is the only stated reason available. Left out: Twilio (−10.62%, the largest decline; MarketBeat cited no company-specific news), Moderna (−7.82%; no Friday reason found) and Northrop (+4.05%) and RTX (+3.73%), which no outlet tied to Friday.

Super Micro (SMCI) −9.86% — what happened: AI hardware and memory fell together: Flex −8.16%, Seagate −7.50%, Coherent −7.06%, Western Digital −6.86%, SanDisk −6.85%, Ciena −6.67%, HPE −5.97%, Micron −5.63%. Stated reason: no Friday news specific to Super Micro surfaced. AP said chip companies pulled back as “worries deepened about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last,” naming Micron and Intel. Trading Economics tied the chip losses partly to modest revenue figures from Anthropic and to worries about higher borrowing costs for heavily indebted companies. Read-through: cycle-level. The selling hit the suppliers to the data-center build-out, the companies that depend on their customers’ spending. That fits the outlets’ financing framing; CL-0042 tests whether it lasts.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) −7.63% — what happened: software and cybersecurity reversed Thursday’s rally: Palantir −7.22%, Datadog −7.19%, CrowdStrike −7.03%, Fortinet −7.03%, ServiceNow −4.44% (after +6.14% Thursday). Stated reason: none surfaced for Friday. The one dated catalyst found, a report that OpenAI was in early talks to buy security firm Trail of Bits, came on Oct 14 (24/7 Wall St.) and is not offered as Friday’s reason. Read-through: Thursday’s “rotation into software” framing didn’t hold for these names on Friday. The broader breadth signal did: the average stock still beat the index (CL-0045).

Intel (INTC) −5.79% — what happened: Intel fell with the chip group on Friday. Stated reason: AP named Intel’s drop in its account of chip stocks falling on AI-buildout worries. This morning Reuters reported Intel up about 4% before the open after JPMorgan upgraded it to neutral from underweight. Intel reports results Oct 29, after the Fed meeting (Intel investor relations). Read-through: a first test of the dip-buying framing in this morning’s futures coverage. One upgrade is a single-name event, not a cycle signal.

Sector note — Energy (XLE) +2.52% vs. SPY −1.11% (+3.63 points); Technology (XLK) −3.02%. Utilities (+1.34%) and consumer staples (+1.08%) also rose. Energy gainers included Targa +4.37%, Diamondback +4.27%, Kinder Morgan +4.21% and APA +4.07%; this system’s search found no company-specific reasons for them. Read-through: on Thursday energy stocks fell while oil rose; on Friday they moved with oil. Utilities and staples rising on a down day fits a defensive tilt; no outlet explained it, so that is a reading, not a finding.
chart_of_day_why: Mechanical rule (§6.5a, largest |z| flag) points to HY OAS for a third session: z +3.36, dated 10-15, ahead of SOFR’s +2.28 and the Russell’s −2.19. Oil (rule c, the dominant story) was the alternative, but the rule order comes first. This time the window is the full 120 days the z-score uses, so the six-month picture is visible: spreads drifted up from late summer, and Wednesday’s 3.25% (marked) sits at the top. For §4F scale: Thursday’s 3.23% is the 75th percentile of the series’ ~3-year record here, not extreme. Tonight’s Friday print grades CL-0048.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (this system’s chip-fund proxy for AI capex) fell 3.41% Friday against SPY’s −1.11%, its ninth straight daily decline. It fell 10.53% for the week and is 19.30% below its Jun 22 high.

The financing story moved from single names toward project debt. Reuters reported Friday that CoreWeave’s shares and bonds were headed for steep weekly losses, and CNBC reported this morning that the stock fell more than 25% last week. Reuters tied the selloff to inflation data that raised bets on rate hikes; this system’s numbers complicate that, since the 2-year fell 3bp Friday and the 10-year fell 15bp for the week. Midweek, Reuters and CNBC reported the cost of insuring CoreWeave’s debt above 1,000bp, meaning more than $10 a year to insure $100 of its bonds. The Financial Times reported Friday, as relayed by other outlets, that some bonds funding data-center construction for Meta, Nvidia and Oracle slipped below face value; Allianz’s chief investment officer called it a “Darwinian moment” for weaker projects. Forbes reported that of roughly $80 billion of data-center bonds sold this year, about $37 billion are rated junk, more than four times last year’s junk total. This system’s search found no new deal priced, pulled or delayed over the weekend, and no hyperscaler change to spending guidance.

Cycle-level reading: the strain is in project and single-name debt, not yet in the broad credit indexes this system tracks: HY OAS was 3.23% on Thursday, down 2bp. Two things this week test that. Friday’s credit print (CL-0048) shows whether index spreads moved on the selloff day. And Meta reports Wednesday after the close (company announcement), a chance to hear a hyperscaler on capital spending. Why this matters: a client in AI stocks is exposed to the cost of credit for the builders as much as to chip demand. When the builders’ debt gets expensive, orders are what’s at risk (§8: cycle-level only).
calendar_note_html:
Today: the homebuilders’ confidence index (NAHB, 10am ET; this system’s calendar shows a forecast of 31 against September’s 32). This week: September housing starts and permits Tuesday (forecasts 1.30 million and 1.39 million, annual pace) and pending home sales (−0.4%); weekly jobless claims Thursday (forecast 200,000); flash purchasing-manager surveys Friday (manufacturing 55.5 from 57.0, services 58.0 from 58.7) and the final University of Michigan sentiment reading. Its preliminary October reading was 46.3, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.7% (Advisor Perspectives’ summary of the University of Michigan data). Earnings: Netflix Tuesday (Hargreaves Lansdown calendar); Tesla (company filing), Meta (company announcement), Texas Instruments and IBM Wednesday after the close. Fed officials stay in their quiet period through Oct 29, ahead of the Oct 27–28 meeting.

Friday’s results: import prices rose 1.1% in September and 8.1% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since July 2022, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics; fuel import prices rose 4.8% on the month. Investinglive put the consensus at +0.8% (this system’s calendar had +0.6%). Industrial production rose 0.7% against 0.4% expected, led by a 3.5% jump in utilities output; factory output rose 0.3% (Federal Reserve). Reuters reported the fiscal-2026 budget deficit at $1.99 trillion, the largest in five years, with debt-service outlays at a record $1.36 trillion.

Why this matters to the current regime: fuel is pushing import prices up, which keeps inflation pressure on the Fed. Interest costs are now a big line in the federal budget, which matters for how much the Treasury borrows. With the Fed quiet until its meeting, this week’s data and earnings carry the story.
concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 3
concept_title: Good news, falling price: “priced in” vs. “improving”
concept_html: Unit 6’s goal is telling “priced in” apart from “improving.” Last week gave a clean example. On Thursday, TSMC, the main contract chipmaker for AI processors, reported third-quarter profit up 68.7% from a year earlier, above the consensus cited in pre-results coverage. The business is improving. Yet the chip fund SMH fell 1.04% that day, 3.41% on Friday and 10.53% for the week, its ninth straight decline. How can both be true? A stock price is a bet on the future, and it already contains what investors expected. When expectations are very high, good news has to beat them by a lot just to hold the price. Last week’s coverage also focused on a different question: whether the customers buying these chips can keep paying for the build-out (Tier 3). So the price was answering a different question from the earnings report. Improving means the business is getting better. Priced in means the price already assumed it would. Surprises come from the gap between the two.
client_translation: A company can report great results and its stock can still fall, because the price already assumed great results; what moves the price is how the news compares with what investors expected.
client_lens_html:
“Is the AI bubble bursting?” The most crowded part of the trade had a hard week: the Nasdaq Composite fell 4.48% and the chip fund SMH 10.53%. But the average S&P stock rose 0.49%, bonds rallied, and broad credit spreads barely moved. The pain is concentrated in the most borrowed AI builders and their suppliers. This week’s tests are Wednesday’s big-tech earnings and whether junk-bond spreads start to widen.

“Oil is over $100 again. What does that mean for me?” WTI closed at $101.41 Friday, up 10.41% for the week, as outlets reported attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. It shows up first at the pump and in prices of imported goods: fuel import prices rose 4.8% in September (BLS). It also keeps the Fed cautious. Over the weekend, a waiver of new Russia sanctions and an Iranian reopening offer pointed the other way, so oil can swing hard on headlines.

“Why hold bonds?” Last week is the answer. While the Nasdaq Composite fell 4.48%, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 15bp, which means bond prices rose. Bonds and stocks don’t always move in opposite directions, but last week they did.
